extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in stand-up comedy and memoir writing; aspiring comedians and comedy writers
extracted.subtask_short: stand-up comedy craft and memoir writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and craft observations about performing stand-up comedy (practice, storytelling, place/attunement, evolution of material) and choices in writing a personal memoir (tense, honesty, editing, structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice / Live performance is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Visibility doesn’t mean anything if you’re not good at what you do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'Visibility doesn’t mean anything if you’re not good at what you do. Whether you’re a musician or a filmmaker or a writer or a performer, you can get all the Twitter followers and Instagram views that you want, but if you’re not putting anything interesting or good up, then what good does that do you? You still have to go do it.' Practical implication: sustained, in-person practice/performing is necessary to develop skill; online visibility cannot substitute for craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location and attunement influence comedic material
rubrics_metrics.description: A performer’s location — and being present/attuned to place and time — shapes their comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes/explanation: 'One of the most interesting things in the book is how your location — Virginia, and then Los Angeles — affected your comedy.' 'You still have to leave your house and live your day to day. And that changes from almost block to block within the same city.' Warning: over-reliance on screens can reduce attunement: 'there are some people who are losing being attuned to their place and time ... because they’re just looking at a screen the whole time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Online visibility doesn’t replace doing the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Being visible online (YouTube, podcasts, followers) is not enough if the underlying work/art is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasized by Oswalt: social media metrics are meaningless without interesting or good material. The practical takeaway is to prioritize craft and continued live performance over seeking only online exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from joke-oriented material to storytelling with age and comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: As comedians age and become more comfortable, their material often shifts from tight joke-telling to personal storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes/explanation: 'Over the years, your comedy has changed from joke-oriented material to storytelling.' 'It happened because I’m getting older and I’m changing... Any comedian that you see over time, if they’re really committed to the craft, it changes pretty radically.' Also: younger performers 'put up shields to look cool' with jokes; older performers 'open yourself up a little bit' and connect with stories. Online culture may make audiences more used to personal narratives, reinforcing the trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy evolves radically with commitment to the craft
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedian who is committed to the craft will change substantially over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'Any comedian that you see over time, if they’re really committed to the craft, it changes pretty radically.' Guidance: expect and accept evolution in voice and material; continual work leads to significant shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of present tense in memoir to recreate moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing a memoir in the present tense helps recreate and inhabit remembered moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oswalt: 'Your book is almost entirely in the present tense... when you remember things, you have to go back into that moment as if you’re living it in the present tense. That’s the only way that it works.' He also frames this partly as surrendering to a personal weakness in grammar/tense, suggesting voice and fidelity to memory can justify tense choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing truthfulness and editing in personal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: There is tension between being truthful/personal and the editorial process of cutting or neatening material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'I was being so truthful. Am I being dishonest by going back and editing and cutting things out? That part was a little difficult.' Practical note: initial writing felt easier than revising; authors may struggle with whether editing diminishes authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interspersing comedic sketches with biographical material
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining less personal comedy sketches with biographical pieces can ease an author into a memoir format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oswalt’s process: his first book 'interspersed it with little comedic bits and short pieces that weren’t very personal' and observed that 'the stuff that tended to stick out and that people liked were the more biographical things.' Implication: readers respond strongly to biographical/personal material; mixing forms can be a transitional strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaining perspective and empathy with age
rubrics_metrics.description: Looking back at younger years often reveals self-centered narratives; maturing brings empathy and recognition that you’re not the 'star' of every story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'You’re the wronged hero of this amazing saga... You’re not the star of this movie.' Practical guidance: reflection through memoir or time in the craft can lead to greater empathy and better, less self-focused material.
